title: Up quark (u)
summary: The lighter of the two quarks that build protons and neutrons: two of them, with one down quark, make a proton.

layers.basics:
Every proton in every atom you have ever touched contains two up quarks and one down quark; every neutron contains one up quark and two down quarks. The up quark has an electric charge of +⅔ (two thirds of a proton's charge, in units where the electron is −1).

You will never see one on its own: the strong force keeps quarks locked inside bigger particles. Its mass is tiny, about 2 MeV/c², so the two up quarks and the down quark together supply only about 1% of the mass of a proton. Most of the rest is energy in the strong force field.

As far as anyone has measured, an up quark has no inside: it is a point-like excitation of a quantum field.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 2.16 ± 0.07 MeV. A "current-quark mass": the parameter in the theory's equations at that energy scale. A free quark is never seen, so there is no scale to put it on; the number depends on the scheme and the energy scale used to define it. Two up quarks and one down quark make a proton.

Lifetime. Up quarks inside protons are as stable as the proton itself (no proton decay has ever been seen; see the proton entry).

Colour charge. Yes. Quarks carry colour charge, the charge of the strong force. It comes in three kinds, called red, green and blue after a loose analogy; there is no real colour involved. Only combinations with no net colour are ever seen, so a lone quark is never observed.

Antiparticle. Anti-up quark (ū). Same mass and spin, opposite electric charge and opposite colour (an "anticolour").

Why one number is not enough. The quoted mass is the "current-quark mass" in the MS-bar scheme at 2 GeV. A confined quark has no scale to weigh it on, so the mass is a parameter whose value depends on the energy scale and the way you define it. The PDG notes that the up and down masses "are not without controversy".

Up and down quarks are the first generation of quarks. The up quark has a roughly twice-as-heavy partner, charm, and a far heavier one, top, with the same charge and spin.
layers.expert:
The up quark is a spin-½ colour triplet. The left-handed field forms a weak-isospin doublet with the down quark (the d′ of the CKM matrix); the right-handed field is a weak-isospin singlet with hypercharge 4/3 (left-handed doublet: 1/3), from Q = T₃ + Y/2 (PDG Electroweak Model review). It couples to gluons, the photon (Q = +2/3), the W (to d, s, b with strengths set by the CKM matrix), the Z and the Higgs field (Yukawa coupling ∝ mass).

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = +1/2. The left-handed version sits in a doublet with a down-type quark; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Evidence for pointlike quark-like constituents inside the proton came from electron scattering at SLAC in 1968–69 (deep inelastic scattering); the up quark was proposed in the quark model of Gell-Mann and of Zweig in 1964.

Where you meet it. Everywhere. Every proton has two up quarks and every neutron has one; together with down quarks they are the only quarks in ordinary stable matter (apart from short-lived quark–antiquark pairs).

facts: MS-bar scheme at a scale of 2 GeV

title: Down quark (d)
summary: The slightly heavier of the two lightest quarks: one in a proton, two in a neutron.

layers.basics:
A proton holds one down quark (and two up quarks); a neutron holds two down quarks (and one up quark). A down quark carries an electric charge of −⅓. Add up the charges: proton u+u+d = ⅔+⅔−⅓ = +1; neutron u+d+d = ⅔−⅓−⅓ = 0.

The down quark is a little heavier than the up quark (about 4.7 MeV/c² against 2.2), which is a large part of why the neutron is slightly heavier than the proton and why a lone neutron decays: one of its down quarks turns into an up quark.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 4.70 ± 0.07 MeV. A "current-quark mass": the parameter in the theory's equations at that energy scale. A free quark is never seen, so there is no scale to put it on; the number depends on the scheme and the energy scale used to define it. It is a little heavier than the up quark, which is why a neutron is slightly heavier than a proton.

Lifetime. Down quarks in stable nuclei are stable; in a free neutron one turns into an up quark by the weak force (see the neutron entry).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • d → u + W⁻ (virtual), as in neutron decay

Colour charge. Yes. Quarks carry colour charge, the charge of the strong force. It comes in three kinds, called red, green and blue after a loose analogy; there is no real colour involved. Only combinations with no net colour are ever seen, so a lone quark is never observed.

Antiparticle. Anti-down quark (d̄). Same mass and spin, opposite electric charge and opposite colour (an "anticolour").

Beta decay. When a neutron decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino, the quark-level event is d → u + W⁻, followed by W⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. The W is "virtual" here: there is not enough energy to make a real one.

The quoted mass is the MS-bar "current-quark mass" at 2 GeV; there is no such thing as weighing a free down quark.
layers.expert:
Spin-½ colour triplet with Q = −1/3. The left-handed field is the lower member of the weak-isospin doublet with the up quark; right-handed hypercharge −2/3. The mass difference md − mu is small compared with the strong-interaction scale, so isospin symmetry (swapping u and d) is a good approximation, and the proton and neutron look almost the same to the strong force.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = -1/2. The left-handed version sits in a doublet with a up-type quark; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Seen indirectly in the same SLAC electron-scattering experiments as the up quark (1968–69); proposed in the 1964 quark model.

Where you meet it. In every proton (one) and every neutron (two). Together with up quarks, the only quarks in ordinary matter.

facts: MS-bar scheme at a scale of 2 GeV
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Strange quark (s)
summary: A heavier cousin of the down quark, found in kaons and in the first "strange" particles seen in cosmic rays.

layers.basics:
The strange quark is like a down quark (charge −⅓) but about twenty times heavier. It does not appear in ordinary stable matter, but the cosmic rays that hit the atmosphere make strange particles all the time, and a proton contains short-lived strange–antistrange pairs as part of its quark sea.

It was named "strange" because the particles that contain it lived surprisingly long for their mass: they decay by the weak force, not the strong one.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 92.9 ± 0.7 MeV. A "current-quark mass": the parameter in the theory's equations at that energy scale. A free quark is never seen, so there is no scale to put it on; the number depends on the scheme and the energy scale used to define it. Roughly 20 times the down-quark mass.

Lifetime. Strange hadrons decay by the weak force: the charged kaon lasts about 1.24×10⁻⁸ s and the Λ about 2.6×10⁻¹⁰ s (PDG).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • s → u + W⁻ (virtual): how a kaon or Λ decays

Colour charge. Yes. Quarks carry colour charge, the charge of the strong force. It comes in three kinds, called red, green and blue after a loose analogy; there is no real colour involved. Only combinations with no net colour are ever seen, so a lone quark is never observed.

Antiparticle. Anti-strange quark (s̄). Same mass and spin, opposite electric charge and opposite colour (an "anticolour").

The quoted mass (92.9 MeV/c²) is MS-bar at 2 GeV. The strange quark is the heaviest quark that is still light compared with the scale of the strong force (about 1 GeV), so it blurs the line between "light" and "heavy" quarks.
layers.expert:
Second generation, down-type. It decays (inside hadrons) through s → u + W⁻ with a rate suppressed by the small CKM element Vus. Strangeness is conserved by the strong and electromagnetic forces but not by the weak force, which is why strange particles are produced in pairs but decay one at a time.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = -1/2. The left-handed version sits in a doublet with a up-type quark; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. The first "strange" particles (kaons) were seen in cosmic-ray cloud-chamber photographs by Rochester and Butler in 1947; the quark picture that explains them came in 1964.

Where you meet it. Made constantly in the debris of cosmic rays hitting the air, and present as short-lived pairs inside every proton, but not part of ordinary stable matter.

facts: MS-bar scheme at a scale of 2 GeV
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Charm quark (c)
summary: The second-generation partner of the up quark: about 600 times as heavy as it, found as the J/ψ in 1974.

layers.basics: The charm quark has the same electric charge as the up quark (+⅔) and the same spin, but a much larger mass, about 1.27 GeV/c², more than a proton. It does not exist in everyday matter. When two groups found a new particle, the J/ψ, in November 1974, it was a charm quark bound to an anti-charm quark.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 1.2729 ± 0.0045 GeV. The "running" mass in the MS-bar scheme evaluated at its own value. The PDG notes the same quark corresponds to a pole mass of about 1.65 GeV in another scheme: the same quark, a different definition.

Lifetime. Charm hadrons decay by the weak force: the D⁰ lasts about 4.1×10⁻¹³ s and the D⁺ about 1.0×10⁻¹² s (PDG).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • c → s + W⁺ (virtual)

Colour charge. Yes. Quarks carry colour charge, the charge of the strong force. It comes in three kinds, called red, green and blue after a loose analogy; there is no real colour involved. Only combinations with no net colour are ever seen, so a lone quark is never observed.

Antiparticle. Anti-charm quark (c̄). Same mass and spin, opposite electric charge and opposite colour (an "anticolour").

The mass is the MS-bar mass at its own scale, 1.2729 ± 0.0045 GeV (PDG 2026). In another scheme the same quark has a "pole mass" of about 1.65 GeV. The J/ψ is surprisingly long-lived for a particle of mass 3.097 GeV: its width is only 92.6 keV (PDG). That narrowness was a key clue.
layers.expert:
Charm decays via c → s + W⁺, dominated by the CKM element Vcs.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = +1/2. The left-handed version sits in a doublet with a down-type quark; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Seen as the J/ψ meson (a charm–anticharm pair) in November 1974 by two groups at once: one led by Burton Richter at SLAC and one led by Samuel Ting at Brookhaven.

Where you meet it. Not in everyday matter. Made in particle accelerators and in cosmic-ray collisions; a very small charm component exists inside the proton.

facts: MS-bar scheme, at the scale of the charm-quark mass itself
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Bottom quark (b)
summary: The heavy cousin of the down and strange quarks, found as the Υ meson in 1977.

layers.basics: The bottom quark has charge −⅓ and a mass of about 4.2 GeV/c², over four times a proton. It was found as part of the Υ (upsilon) particle, a bottom–antibottom pair, at Fermilab in 1977. Its relatives, the B mesons, are made in huge numbers by "B factory" colliders because they decay in ways that differ for matter and antimatter.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 4.186 ± 0.006 GeV. The "running" mass in the MS-bar scheme at its own scale; other definitions (pole mass) give a larger number, because the quark mass depends on how and at what energy you define it.

Lifetime. B mesons decay by the weak force: the B⁺ lasts about 1.64×10⁻¹² s and the B⁰ about 1.51×10⁻¹² s (PDG).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • b → c + W⁻ (virtual)

Colour charge. Yes. Quarks carry colour charge, the charge of the strong force. It comes in three kinds, called red, green and blue after a loose analogy; there is no real colour involved. Only combinations with no net colour are ever seen, so a lone quark is never observed.

Antiparticle. Anti-bottom quark (b̄). Same mass and spin, opposite electric charge and opposite colour (an "anticolour").

B mesons live about 1.5 picoseconds (1.5×10⁻¹² s), long enough to travel a fraction of a millimetre before decaying, which lets detectors see the decay point.
layers.expert:
Third generation, down-type. It decays via b → c + W⁻, suppressed by the small CKM element Vcb, which is why its lifetime is long for a particle of its mass. CP violation (a difference between matter and antimatter) is large in some B decays.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = -1/2. The left-handed version sits in a doublet with a up-type quark; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Seen as the Υ (upsilon) meson, a bottom–antibottom pair, in 1977 by an experiment led by Leon Lederman at Fermilab.

Where you meet it. Only in accelerators and rare cosmic-ray collisions. B mesons are made by the billion in dedicated "B factory" colliders to study matter–antimatter differences.

facts: MS-bar scheme, at the scale of the bottom-quark mass itself
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Top quark (t)
summary: The heaviest known elementary particle: about as heavy as a gold atom, but it lasts less than a trillionth of a trillionth of a second.

layers.basics: The top quark has charge +⅔ and a mass of about 172.6 GeV/c², about 184 times a proton and about 340,000 times an electron. It was found in 1995 at Fermilab. It decays so fast (about 5×10⁻²⁵ s) that it falls apart before it can bind with other quarks, so it is the only quark we study almost bare.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 172.60 ± 0.27 GeV. This is the one quark mass measured directly from the energies of the particles it decays into. Because the top decays before it can bind into a hadron, it is the only quark we can study "almost bare". The PDG notes that turning this number into a precise theoretical mass (pole or MS-bar) carries a theory uncertainty that is hard to quantify.

Lifetime. About 5×10⁻²⁵ s, from the measured decay width of 1.42 GeV (lifetime = ħ / width; my calculation). It decays before it can form a hadron.

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • t → W⁺ + b  (0.957 ± 0.034 of decays)

Colour charge. Yes. Quarks carry colour charge, the charge of the strong force. It comes in three kinds, called red, green and blue after a loose analogy; there is no real colour involved. Only combinations with no net colour are ever seen, so a lone quark is never observed.

Antiparticle. Anti-top quark (t̄). Same mass and spin, opposite electric charge and opposite colour (an "anticolour").

Quark mass, three ways. The PDG lists the top mass from direct measurements as 172.60 ± 0.27 GeV. It also lists a value from the cross-section of making top pairs interpreted as an MS-bar mass (162.5 +2.1/−1.5 GeV) and as a pole mass (172.1 ± 0.6 GeV). They are different definitions of the same quark, and the "direct" value comes from the kinematics of its decay products, which is as close to a weight as a quark gets.

The width, 1.42 GeV, is large, so the particle is very short-lived and hardly a "particle" in the everyday sense.
layers.expert:
The top's large mass means its Yukawa coupling to the Higgs field is close to 1, much stronger than any other fermion. Loops with top quarks dominate quantum corrections to the Higgs mass, which is part of the hierarchy problem. Its decay t → W b has a measured ratio Γ(Wb)/Γ(Wq) = 0.957 ± 0.034 (PDG), consistent with 1.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = +1/2. The left-handed version sits in a doublet with a down-type quark; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Announced on 2 March 1995 by the CDF and DØ collaborations at Fermilab's Tevatron proton–antiproton collider.

Where you meet it. Not in everyday matter and gone within 10⁻²⁴ s of being made. Made by the million at the LHC. It is the heaviest known elementary particle.

facts: Direct measurements: reconstructed from the decay products of top–antitop pairs (Tevatron and LHC average)
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Electron (e⁻)
summary: The light, negatively charged particle that surrounds every atomic nucleus and carries electric current.

layers.basics:
The electron is the particle that makes chemistry: electrons arranged around nuclei decide how atoms bond, and electrons moving through wires are electric current. It has charge −1, a mass of 0.511 MeV/c² (1/1836 of a proton), and no known inside.

All electrons are exactly alike. In the Standard Model that is because they are all excitations of the same electron field.

The electron appears in the atom cards of this explorer: its cloud is a probability pattern, not a little ball in orbit.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 0.51099895069 ± 0.00000000016 MeV. A directly measured rest mass, known to better than a part in 10⁹. Unlike a quark mass it has an ordinary meaning, though the Higgs field is what gives it a mass at all.

Lifetime. Stable as far as anyone can tell. PDG: mean life > 6.6×10²⁸ years (90% confidence) for decay into a neutrino and photon.

Colour charge. No. Leptons carry no colour charge, so they do not feel the strong force at all.

Antiparticle. Positron (e⁺). Proposed from Dirac's relativistic theory of the electron and found in cosmic rays by Carl Anderson in 1932. Same mass, charge +1.

The electron is the lightest charged particle, so it cannot decay: charge conservation would forbid it. The PDG gives a lower bound on its lifetime of 6.6×10²⁸ years (90% confidence) for decay into a neutrino and a photon.

Its magnetic moment is one of the most precisely measured quantities in physics (see the PDG listing). Its mass comes from its coupling to the Higgs field; without that coupling an electron would have no mass and atoms would not hold together.
layers.expert:
Spin-½ Dirac fermion, member of the first-generation lepton doublet (νₑ, e)L, with the right-handed electron an SU(2) singlet of hypercharge −2. Couples to the photon (Q = −1), the Z, the W (to νₑ) and the Higgs (Yukawa y_e = √2 mₑ / v, with v ≈ 246 GeV from the PDG).

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = -1/2. The left-handed version is the lower member of a doublet with the matching neutrino; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. J. J. Thomson at the Cavendish Laboratory in 1897, measuring the charge-to-mass ratio of cathode rays and showing they were far lighter than any atom.

Where you meet it. The cloud around every atom: all of chemistry, the current in a wire and the light from a screen. About as many as there are protons in everything you touch.

facts: Measured directly (Penning-trap and atomic-physics experiments); no scheme needed because the electron is not confined
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Muon (μ⁻)
summary: A heavier copy of the electron that decays in about two microseconds; cosmic-ray muons pass through you constantly.

layers.basics: The muon is a heavier twin of the electron: same charge (−1), same kind of behaviour, but about 207 times the mass. It lives for only 2.2 microseconds, yet muons made when cosmic rays hit the upper air arrive at ground level, roughly one per square centimetre per minute on a horizontal surface at sea level.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 105.6583755 ± 0.0000023 MeV. A directly measured rest mass, about 207 times the electron's. The reason there is a second, heavier copy of the electron is not known.

Lifetime. Mean life 2.1969811×10⁻⁶ s (PDG).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + ν_μ

Colour charge. No. Leptons carry no colour charge, so they do not feel the strong force at all.

Antiparticle. Antimuon (μ⁺). Same mass and lifetime, charge +1.

They reach the ground because of time dilation: a muon moving at nearly the speed of light has its lifetime stretched in our frame. It decays almost always into an electron and two neutrinos (μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + ν_μ). The muon is also at the centre of the "g−2" experiments: see the frontier note on the muon magnetic moment.
layers.expert:
Second-generation charged lepton. Its magnetic moment anomaly is measured to 127 parts per billion by Fermilab's final result (2025), and the PDG review has a dedicated section. As recorded in the frontier file, the 2025 Standard Model prediction agrees with the measurement; the earlier discrepancy has largely gone.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = -1/2. The left-handed version is the lower member of a doublet with the matching neutrino; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Seth Neddermeyer and Carl Anderson (and, independently, Jabez Street and Edward Stevenson) in cosmic-ray cloud-chamber tracks, reported in 1937.

Where you meet it. Cosmic-ray muons pass through you all the time: roughly one per square centimetre of horizontal surface per minute at sea level (PDG cosmic-ray review, 2000 edition).

facts: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026
open_questions: Why does a second, heavier copy of the electron exist? The theory does not say.

title: Tau lepton (τ⁻)
summary: The heaviest charged lepton: a copy of the electron about 3,500 times as heavy, living a third of a trillionth of a second.

layers.basics: The tau has the electron's charge (−1) but weighs about 3,477 times as much (1.777 GeV/c²), more than a proton. Because it is so heavy it can decay into hadrons as well as leptons. It lives about 2.9×10⁻¹³ seconds.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 1776.93 ± 0.09 MeV. A directly measured rest mass, about 3,477 times the electron's (a ratio: my calculation). The heaviest charged lepton, heavy enough to decay into hadrons.

Lifetime. Mean life 2.903×10⁻¹³ s (PDG).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • τ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + ν_τ  ((17.85 ± 0.04)×10⁻² of decays)
  • τ⁻ → μ⁻ + ν̄_μ + ν_τ  ((17.37 ± 0.04)×10⁻² of decays)
  • τ⁻ → π⁻ + ν_τ  ((10.82 ± 0.05)×10⁻² of decays)
  • τ⁻ → π⁻ + π⁰ + ν_τ  ((25.49 ± 0.09)×10⁻² of decays)

Colour charge. No. Leptons carry no colour charge, so they do not feel the strong force at all.

Antiparticle. Antitau (τ⁺). Same mass and lifetime, charge +1.

Martin Perl's group found it at SLAC in 1975 by seeing electron–muon pairs with missing energy that no known process could explain. About 17% of tau decays are to an electron and two neutrinos, about 17% to a muon and two neutrinos, and the rest involve pions (PDG 2026).
layers.expert:
Third-generation charged lepton. Lepton universality is the statement that the electron, muon and tau couple identically to the W and Z apart from their masses. The PDG 2026 W branching fractions are 10.71 ± 0.16% (eν), 10.63 ± 0.15% (μν) and 11.38 ± 0.21% (τν); the tau value sits about 3 combined standard errors above the muon value, a spread the PDG lists and that is still being tested.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = -1/2. The left-handed version is the lower member of a doublet with the matching neutrino; the right-handed version has weak isospin 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Martin Perl and colleagues using the Mark I detector at the SPEAR electron–positron collider at SLAC, 1975, from events containing an electron and a muon with energy missing; he shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

Where you meet it. Not in everyday matter: it lives about 3×10⁻¹³ s. Made in accelerators and by cosmic rays.

facts: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Electron neutrino (νₑ)
summary: A nearly massless, uncharged particle that passes through the Earth almost untouched; its mass is still unknown.

layers.basics:
The electron neutrino is made alongside a electron in weak decays. It has no electric charge and feels only the weak force (and gravity), so it almost never interacts with matter. About 6×10¹⁰ solar neutrinos of the commonest kind pass through every square centimetre of you each second (PDG), unnoticed.

Neutrinos have mass, but it is so small that no experiment has yet weighed one: only upper bounds exist.
layers.deeper:
Mass. Not known. Neutrinos have a tiny mass (oscillation proves it is not zero) but only differences between their squared masses are measured, plus upper bounds on the size. See the neutrino numbers below. Each neutrino of definite flavour is a mix of three mass states (ν₁, ν₂, ν₃); that is what neutrino oscillation shows. The original Standard Model had massless neutrinos, so their mass is the first thing found that goes beyond it.

Lifetime. No decay has been observed. Heavier neutrino mass states could in principle decay into lighter ones; the PDG gives limits on the lifetime-to-mass ratio.

Colour charge. No. Leptons carry no colour charge, so they do not feel the strong force at all.

Antiparticle. Antineutrino (ν̄ₑ). OPEN QUESTION: is the antineutrino a different particle (Dirac neutrino) or the same particle as the neutrino (Majorana)? Not yet known; experiments searching for neutrinoless double-beta decay test this.

What is known. Neutrinos change flavour as they travel (oscillation), which proves they have mass and that the flavour states are mixtures of three mass states. Oscillations measure only differences of squared masses: Δm²₂₁ = (7.60 ± 0.17)×10⁻⁵ eV² and |Δm²₃₂| ≈ 2.4–2.5×10⁻³ eV² (PDG 2026; the sign, normal or inverted ordering, is not yet known).

Upper bounds. KATRIN's 2025 result: the effective electron-antineutrino mass is below 0.45 eV at 90% confidence (see frontier note katrin_neutrino). From cosmology, the sum of the three masses is below about 0.064 eV at 95% confidence for the standard cosmological model with DESI DR2 data (listed in the PDG 2026), and the bound depends on the cosmological model assumed. From oscillations alone the sum is at least about 0.058 eV (normal) or 0.10 eV (inverted), by my arithmetic from the PDG numbers.

Open questions. The absolute mass scale, the ordering, whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles, and whether the CP-violating phase is nonzero.
layers.expert:
Three mass states ν₁, ν₂, ν₃ mix through the PMNS matrix with measured angles sin²θ₁₂ = 0.307 ± 0.012, sin²θ₁₃ = 0.0217 ± 0.0007 and sin²θ₂₃ ≈ 0.53 (PDG 2026, normal ordering). Only left-handed neutrinos (and right-handed antineutrinos) have been seen. A neutrino mass term needs either right-handed partners (Dirac mass) or a lepton-number-violating Majorana term; which is realised is unknown. Neutrinoless double-beta decay is the main test of the second.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = +1/2. Only the left-handed neutrino has been observed; it forms a doublet with the electron.

Discovery. Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines detected (anti)neutrinos from a nuclear reactor at the Savannah River Plant, South Carolina, in 1956, by the flash from inverse beta decay.

Where you meet it. The Sun's fusion makes of order 10³⁸ of them every second (my estimate from its luminosity); roughly 6×10¹⁰ of the most common (pp) kind pass through each square centimetre of Earth per second, and you notice none (PDG, solar-neutrino section of the neutrino-mixing review).

facts: Not known. Neutrinos have a tiny mass (oscillation proves it is not zero) but only differences between their squared masses are measured, plus upper bounds on the size. See the neutrino numbers below.
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026
open_questions: What are the neutrino masses (only bounds exist)?
Is the mass ordering normal or inverted?
Is the neutrino its own antiparticle (Majorana) or not (Dirac)?

What is known. Neutrinos change flavour as they travel (oscillation), which proves they have mass and that the flavour states are mixtures of three mass states. Oscillations measure only differences of squared masses: Δm²₂₁ = (7.60 ± 0.17)×10⁻⁵ eV² and |Δm²₃₂| ≈ 2.4–2.5×10⁻³ eV² (PDG 2026; the sign, normal or inverted ordering, is not yet known).

From cosmology, the sum of the three masses is below about 0.064 eV at 95% confidence for the standard cosmological model with DESI DR2 data (listed in the PDG 2026), and the bound depends on the cosmological model assumed. From oscillations alone the sum is at least about 0.058 eV (normal) or 0.10 eV (inverted), by my arithmetic from the PDG numbers.

layers.expert:
Three mass states ν₁, ν₂, ν₃ mix through the PMNS matrix with measured angles sin²θ₁₂ = 0.307 ± 0.012, sin²θ₁₃ = 0.0217 ± 0.0007 and sin²θ₂₃ ≈ 0.53 (PDG 2026, normal ordering). Only left-handed neutrinos (and right-handed antineutrinos) have been seen. A neutrino mass term needs either right-handed partners (Dirac mass) or a lepton-number-violating Majorana term; which is realised is unknown. Neutrinoless double-beta decay is the main test of the second.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = +1/2. Only the left-handed neutrino has been observed; it forms a doublet with the muon.

Discovery. Leon Lederman, Melvin Schwartz and Jack Steinberger at Brookhaven's Alternating Gradient Synchrotron in 1962 showed that the neutrino made with a muon is a different kind from the one made with an electron.

Where you meet it. Made when cosmic rays hit the upper atmosphere (pions decay to muons and muon neutrinos); studied by the Super-Kamiokande detector.

facts: Not known. Neutrinos have a tiny mass (oscillation proves it is not zero) but only differences between their squared masses are measured, plus upper bounds on the size. See the neutrino numbers below.

title: Tau neutrino (ν_τ)
summary: A nearly massless, uncharged particle that passes through the Earth almost untouched; its mass is still unknown.

layers.basics:
The tau neutrino is made alongside a tau lepton in weak decays. It has no electric charge and feels only the weak force (and gravity), so it almost never interacts with matter. About 6×10¹⁰ solar neutrinos of the commonest kind pass through every square centimetre of you each second (PDG), unnoticed.

Neutrinos have mass, but it is so small that no experiment has yet weighed one: only upper bounds exist.
layers.deeper:

See the neutrino numbers below. Each neutrino of definite flavour is a mix of three mass states (ν₁, ν₂, ν₃); that is what neutrino oscillation shows. The original Standard Model had massless neutrinos, so their mass is the first thing found that goes beyond it.

title: Gluon (g)
summary: The carrier of the strong force: it glues quarks together, and it carries the colour charge it acts on.

layers.basics:
A gluon is a particle of the strong force, the "glue" that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons. It has no mass and no electric charge, but it does carry colour charge (the strong force's kind of charge). Because gluons carry colour themselves, they pull on each other too, which is why the strong force acts very differently from electromagnetism and why quarks can never be pulled apart.

Most of the proton's mass is not the quarks: it is the energy of the gluon field holding them together.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 0 in the Standard Model (the theory's symmetry requires it); a single gluon is never seen alone, so no direct limit can be measured the way it is for the photon.. Gluons are massless in the theory, yet they supply most of the mass of the proton through the energy of the strong field they carry.

Lifetime. Not defined: gluons are never free. They exist only inside hadrons and in short-lived jets.

Colour charge. Yes, unlike the photon. A gluon carries a colour and an anticolour at once; there are eight kinds. Because gluons carry colour, they attract each other, which is why the strong force behaves so differently from electromagnetism.

Antiparticle. Gluon (g). Each of the 8 gluons' antiparticles is again one of the 8 gluon states (a colour–anticolour mixture), so the set is its own antiparticle.

There are eight gluons (eight colour–anticolour combinations). A single gluon is never seen on its own; the first evidence came in 1979 from collision events at the PETRA collider in Hamburg in which a quark and antiquark flew out with a third spray (jet) of particles, a gluon, radiated from one of them.

Lattice calculations indicate gluons carry about half of the proton's momentum (51% in a 2022 calculation at 2 GeV).
layers.expert:
Massless spin-1 gauge bosons of SU(3) colour. The theory has self-interaction vertices (three and four gluons) with colour factor C_A = 3; the PDG notes a measured world average C_A = 2.89 ± 0.03 (stat) ± 0.21 (syst), consistent with the SU(3) value. Whether the gluon field has a mass gap and confines colour is the subject of a Clay Millennium Prize problem (Yang–Mills existence and mass gap), unsolved in rigorous mathematics even though lattice calculations support it.

Weak isospin. T = 0, T₃ = 0. A gluon has no weak isospin.

Discovery. Seen as a third "jet" in electron–positron collisions at the PETRA collider at DESY, Hamburg, in 1979 (TASSO first, then JADE, PLUTO and Mark J).

Where you meet it. Inside every proton and neutron, in all matter, holding quarks together. Gluon energy is most of the mass you weigh.

facts: 0 in the Standard Model (the theory's symmetry requires it); a single gluon is never seen alone, so no direct limit can be measured the way it is for the photon.
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026
open_questions: Why does the theory confine colour at all, and can that be proved mathematically?

title: Photon (γ)
summary: The particle of light, and the carrier of the electromagnetic force.

layers.basics: A photon is the smallest possible bundle of light, and also of any electric or magnetic force between charged particles. It has no mass, no charge, and always moves at the speed of light. Sunlight on the park is a stream of photons; so are radio waves and X-rays, with different energies.
layers.deeper:
Mass. Zero in the Standard Model. PDG: experimental upper limit < 1×10⁻¹⁸ eV.. An upper limit, not a measurement of a mass.

Lifetime. Stable. PDG also gives a photon charge limit of < 1×10⁻⁴⁶ e.

Colour charge. No. Photons carry no colour and do not feel the strong force.

Antiparticle. Photon (γ). The photon is its own antiparticle.

The PDG limit on a photon mass is below 10⁻¹⁸ eV, and on its charge below 10⁻⁴⁶ of an electron's. It is its own antiparticle, and it carries spin 1 (two polarisations, because it is massless). A photon's energy is E = hf: radio photons have very little, gamma rays enormous amounts.
layers.expert:
Gauge boson of the U(1) electromagnetic symmetry that survives after electroweak symmetry breaking; it is a mixture of the SU(2) boson W³ and the hypercharge boson B. Quantum electrodynamics (QED), the quantum theory of photons and charges, predicts the electron magnetic moment to parts per trillion.

Weak isospin. T = 0, T₃ = 0. After electroweak mixing the photon is a combination of the weak-isospin boson W³ and the hypercharge boson B; it has no definite weak isospin.

Discovery. The idea of light as quanta is Planck (1900) and Einstein (1905); Arthur Compton's 1923 X-ray scattering experiments showed light carries momentum like a particle.

Where you meet it. All light, radio, X-rays, and every electric and magnetic force between charges. Sunlight on the park is a stream of photons.

facts: Zero in the Standard Model. PDG: experimental upper limit < 1×10⁻¹⁸ eV.
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: W boson (W±)
summary: A heavy carrier of the weak force that changes one kind of particle into another; it is why the Sun shines slowly.

layers.basics: The W boson (W⁺ and W⁻) carries the weak force, the one responsible for radioactive beta decay and for turning protons into neutrons in the Sun's core. It is charged (±1), and heavy: about 86 times a proton. Its heaviness means the weak force reaches only about 2×10⁻¹⁸ m, so it is "weak" in the sense of being short-ranged and rare.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 80.3625 ± 0.0077 GeV. About 86 times a proton's mass. The W is heavy because the Higgs field gives it mass; that makes the weak force short-ranged.

Lifetime. Decay width 2.14 ± 0.05 GeV (PDG), a lifetime of about 3×10⁻²⁵ s (calculation).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • W⁺ → hadrons (a quark and an antiquark)  ((67.41 ± 0.27)×10⁻² of decays)
  • W⁺ → ℓ⁺ + ν (each of e, μ, τ about equally)  ((10.86 ± 0.09)×10⁻² of decays)

Colour charge. No. W bosons carry no colour.

Antiparticle. W⁻ (W⁻). W⁺ and W⁻ are each other's antiparticles.

The W changes quark flavour (up ↔ down, for example) and turns charged leptons into their neutrinos. Its mass, 80.3625 ± 0.0077 GeV, is the world average of LHC and Tevatron measurements (PDG 2026). It decays within about 3×10⁻²⁵ s: roughly two thirds to quark pairs (67.41%) and the rest to a lepton and its neutrino (10.86% for each of e, μ, τ).
layers.expert:
Spin-1 gauge boson of the SU(2) weak-isospin symmetry; it acquires mass through the Higgs mechanism with m_W = g v / 2 (tree level). The W couples only to left-handed fermions (and right-handed antifermions): the weak force violates mirror symmetry maximally.

Weak isospin. T = 1, T₃ = ±1. W⁺ has T3 = +1, W⁻ has T3 = −1.

Discovery. Announced at CERN in January 1983 by the UA1 and UA2 experiments at the Super Proton Synchrotron run as a proton–antiproton collider (UA1 led by Carlo Rubbia, UA2 by Pierre Darriulat).

Where you meet it. In the Sun's core, a proton turns into a neutron through a virtual W; that step makes hydrogen fusion slow and the Sun last billions of years. Also in radioactive beta decay.

facts: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Z boson (Z⁰)
summary: The neutral heavy carrier of the weak force; its decays showed that there are three light kinds of neutrino.

layers.basics: The Z boson is the electrically neutral partner of the W. It makes the weak force act without changing what a particle is: a neutrino bouncing off matter through a Z leaves as the same neutrino. It weighs about 97 protons and lives about 2.6×10⁻²⁵ s.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 91.1879 ± 0.0020 GeV. About 97 times a proton's mass.

Lifetime. Decay width 2.4955 ± 0.0023 GeV (PDG), a lifetime of about 2.6×10⁻²⁵ s (calculation).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • Z⁰ → hadrons (quark–antiquark)  ((69.911 ± 0.056)×10⁻² of decays)
  • Z⁰ → neutrino + antineutrino (unseen)  ((20.000 ± 0.055)×10⁻² of decays)
  • Z⁰ → ℓ⁺ + ℓ⁻ (each of e, μ, τ)  ((3.3658 ± 0.0023)×10⁻² of decays)

Colour charge. No. The Z carries no colour.

Antiparticle. Z⁰ (Z⁰). The Z is its own antiparticle.

Mass 91.1879 ± 0.0020 GeV; decay width 2.4955 ± 0.0023 GeV (PDG 2026). About 70% of Z decays are to quarks, about 20% to neutrino pairs you cannot see, and about 10% to charged lepton pairs. The invisible fraction, measured at the LEP collider at CERN, fits three light kinds of neutrino.
layers.expert:
A mixture of the SU(2) boson W³ and hypercharge boson B, with mixing angle θ_W. Its coupling to a fermion is set by T₃ − Q sin²θ_W (vector) and T₃ (axial) (PDG Electroweak Model review, eq. 10.7).

Weak isospin. T = 1, T₃ = 0. The Z is a mixture of W³ and the hypercharge boson B. It couples to a fermion through the fermion's T3 and charge.

Discovery. Announced at CERN in 1983 by UA1 and UA2, a few months after the W.

Where you meet it. Mediates the weak "neutral current": neutrinos scattering off matter without changing into charged leptons. Its decays were measured precisely at LEP in the 1990s.

facts: Direct measurements: the position of the resonance in electron–positron collisions at LEP
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Higgs boson (H)
summary: A ripple in the Higgs field, the field that gives the other fundamental particles their mass.

layers.basics:
The Higgs boson is the particle you get when you disturb the Higgs field, a field that has a nonzero value everywhere in the universe. Particles that interact with that field acquire a rest mass; the stronger the interaction, the heavier the particle. The Higgs boson itself weighs about 125 GeV/c², about 133 proton masses, and lasts only about 2×10⁻²² s.

It was announced on 4 July 2012 by the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN.
layers.deeper:
Mass. 125.13 ± 0.11 GeV. About 133 times a proton's mass. A direct measurement from the energies of its decay products.

Lifetime. Decay width 3.0 (+1.5, −0.7) MeV (PDG), a lifetime of about 2×10⁻²² s (calculation).

Main ways it decays (branching fractions from the PDG, 2026):

  • H → b + b̄  ((53 ± 8)×10⁻² of decays)
  • H → W + W*  ((25.7 ± 2.5)×10⁻² of decays)
  • H → τ⁺ + τ⁻  ((6.0 +0.8 −0.7)×10⁻² of decays)
  • H → Z + Z*  ((2.80 ± 0.30)×10⁻² of decays)
  • H → γ + γ  ((2.50 ± 0.20)×10⁻³ of decays)

Colour charge. No.

Antiparticle. Higgs boson (H). The Higgs boson is neutral and is its own antiparticle.

The Higgs gives mass to the electron, the quarks, and the W and Z. It does not explain most of the mass you weigh: about 99% of a proton's mass is the energy of the strong field, not Higgs-given quark masses (see the card on where the proton's mass comes from).

Its decays: to bottom quarks about 53%, W pairs about 26%, tau pairs about 6%, Z pairs about 3%, and two photons about 0.25% (PDG 2026 averages; large uncertainties on the larger rates).
layers.expert:
A neutral spin-0 scalar: the remnant of the complex SU(2) doublet φ after electroweak symmetry breaking with a vacuum value v ≈ 246 GeV (PDG). The couplings of the Higgs to other particles are proportional to their masses and are being measured at the LHC; so far they agree with the Standard Model within the current precision. The Higgs width, 3.0 (+1.5, −0.7) MeV, is not directly measured; it is inferred from other measurements.

Weak isospin. T = 1/2, T₃ = -1/2. The Higgs field is a doublet of weak isospin 1/2; the Higgs boson is what is left of it after the field takes a value everywhere (PDG Electroweak Model review).

Discovery. Announced on 4 July 2012 at CERN by the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider; Peter Higgs and François Englert shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics for the theory.

Where you meet it. Not found alone in ordinary matter: it lives about 10⁻²² s. The Higgs field, which fills space, gives the electron its mass, and therefore sets the size of atoms.

facts: Direct measurements: ATLAS and CMS combined
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026
open_questions: Is the Higgs boson elementary, or made of something? (Not known; no sign of structure.)
Why is its mass so much lighter than quantum corrections would naturally make it (the hierarchy problem)?

title: The Standard Model
summary: The tested description of every known elementary particle and three of the four forces: seventeen particles, one framework, and a list of what it cannot explain.

layers.basics:
Everything you can touch, and nearly everything experiments have made, is built from a short list of elementary particles: the smallest things we have found, with no measured parts. Twelve of them are matter particles (six quarks and six leptons, in three similar families called generations), four carry the forces (the gluon, the photon, the W and the Z), and one, the Higgs boson, is connected to how the others get their mass.

Ordinary matter needs only three of them: the up quark, the down quark and the electron. Quarks make protons and neutrons; protons, neutrons and electrons make atoms.

The picture on this level is not a place. It is the list of everything matter and the forces (except gravity) are made of, as far as experiments have reached.
layers.deeper:
The Standard Model is a quantum field theory built on the symmetry group SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1): SU(3) for the strong force, and SU(2) × U(1) for the electroweak force, which at low energy separates into electromagnetism and the weak force. It makes predictions that have been tested over a huge range of energies.

It has a known gap: gravity is not in it. And it needs about 19 numbers (masses, mixing angles, the strengths of the forces) that must be measured rather than predicted.
layers.expert:
The Lagrangian has four parts: gauge-field kinetic terms, fermion kinetic terms with gauge couplings, the Higgs doublet's kinetic and potential terms, and Yukawa couplings of the Higgs to fermions. The Higgs field's nonzero vacuum value v ≈ 246 GeV (PDG) breaks SU(2) × U(1) to U(1)em and gives masses to W, Z and the charged fermions. Neutrino masses and mixing require an extension.

All values in this explorer come from the Particle Data Group's Review of Particle Physics, 2026 edition (F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011).

facts: 17: 6 quarks, 6 leptons, 4 gauge bosons (counting the gluon, photon, W and Z), 1 Higgs boson
strong, electromagnetic, weak (and the Higgs field)
gravity; dark matter; dark energy; a mechanism for neutrino masses
about 19 (a counting convention; see "What the Standard Model leaves out")
open_questions: Gravity, dark matter, dark energy and the matter–antimatter imbalance are not explained by the Standard Model.

title: Quantum fields: what a particle is
summary: In the Standard Model a particle is not a tiny ball: it is the smallest possible ripple in a field that fills all of space.

layers.basics:
It is natural to picture an electron as a tiny ball. The Standard Model describes it differently: there is an electron field everywhere in space, and an electron is a single, indivisible ripple in that field. Every electron in the universe is the same because they are all ripples in one field. The same goes for every other particle: quarks, photons, the Higgs. Each kind has its own field.

This is why all electrons are identical, and why particles can be created and destroyed (a ripple can start or stop) while the fields stay.

The "ball" picture is a handy approximation when a particle is far from others; the field picture is the one the theory uses.
layers.deeper:
A field has a value at every point. In quantum theory the ways a field can vibrate come in steps: the smallest step is one particle, the next is two, and so on. That is what "quantum" means here: a field cannot hold half a particle.

Nothing here has a definite position until it is measured, so "a ripple" does not mean a hump with edges. It means something that, when probed, shows up as one particle with a certain probability at a certain place.
layers.expert: In quantum field theory the state space is a Fock space built from a vacuum by creation operators; particle number is not conserved in general, but charges (like electric charge) are. Interactions appear as terms coupling different fields. Perturbation theory organises calculations by Feynman diagrams (see that card); the diagram's internal lines are terms in the series, not trajectories.

facts: 12 matter fields (6 quarks, 6 leptons), 4 kinds of force field (gluon, photon, W/Z), 1 Higgs field
each is an excitation of the same electron field
open_questions: What is the best interpretation of quantum fields? The mathematics is settled and tested; what it says about reality is still argued.

title: The four interactions
summary: Four ways particles act on each other: strong, electromagnetic, weak and gravity; the Standard Model includes the first three.

layers.basics:
Everything that happens, from a falling apple to a star burning, comes from four interactions. The strong force binds quarks into protons and neutrons. The electromagnetic force acts between electric charges and makes light. The weak force changes particles into other particles (it makes radioactive beta decay and powers the Sun's slow fusion). Gravity pulls mass together.

The first three are carried by particles: gluons, photons, and the W and Z. Gravity is described by Einstein's general relativity, which is not part of the Standard Model.
layers.deeper: An interaction can be thought of as a coupling between a kind of "charge" and a force-carrying field. For the strong force the charge is colour; for electromagnetism it is electric charge; for the weak force it is weak isospin; the Higgs field couples to mass.
layers.expert: The three Standard Model forces are gauge interactions: local symmetries SU(3)c, SU(2)L and U(1)Y whose gauge bosons (8 gluons, W¹,²,³, B) mediate the forces. After the Higgs field acquires a vacuum value, W³ and B mix into the massless photon and the massive Z.

facts: carrier: gluon · couples to colour charge · acts on quarks and gluons
carrier: photon · couples to electric charge · long range
carriers: W⁺, W⁻, Z · couples to weak isospin · range about 2×10⁻¹⁸ m
not in the Standard Model · acts on all energy

title: The strong force
summary: The strongest known force: it holds quarks inside protons and neutrons, and its leftover holds nuclei together.

layers.basics:
The strong force acts on quarks. It is carried by gluons, and the "charge" it acts on is called colour, a name that has nothing to do with the colours you see. It is so strong that quarks are never found alone: pulling two apart takes so much energy that the energy turns into a new quark–antiquark pair instead.

Inside a proton the quarks are held by it. A faint leftover of the strong force (like the leftover attraction between neutral molecules) holds protons and neutrons together in nuclei.
layers.deeper: The strong force is described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Its strength, written αs, depends on the energy of the process: it is about 0.118 at the energy of the Z boson but grows large below about 1 GeV (PDG QCD review), the scale of the proton. Because the coupling is strong at proton scales, calculations there need supercomputer "lattice" methods.
layers.expert: QCD is the SU(3) gauge theory of colour with quarks in the triplet representation. Its colour factors are C_F = 4/3 and C_A = 3; the PDG quotes a measured C_A = 2.89 ± 0.03 (stat) ± 0.21 (syst) and C_F = 1.30 ± 0.01 ± 0.09, consistent with SU(3). Confinement is observed in lattice calculations but is not mathematically proved from the equations.

title: Colour charge and confinement
summary: Quarks carry a kind of charge called colour, and only colourless combinations exist alone, so a quark can never be pulled out of a proton.

layers.basics:
Quarks carry colour charge: one of three kinds, called red, green and blue as a loose analogy (they are not coloured). Just as electric charge can be positive or negative, a colour has a matching anticolour. In nature we only find combinations with no net colour: a baryon is one quark of each colour, a meson is a colour and its anticolour. This is why free quarks are never seen: confinement.

Try to pull a quark out of a proton and the energy stored in the stretched gluon field becomes enough to create a new quark–antiquark pair, giving a new particle instead of a free quark.
layers.deeper:
"Colourless" means a combination that is unchanged by changing the labels, in the way a mix of red, green and blue light looks white. That is where the combination rules for hadrons (see "Hadrons") come from: three quarks, a quark and an antiquark, and (rarer) exotic combinations.

Colour also resolved a puzzle: the Δ⁺⁺ particle has three identical up quarks with parallel spins, which the exclusion principle forbids unless quarks have another property to tell them apart.
layers.expert: Colour confinement follows from the strong coupling at long distances and is seen in lattice QCD as a linearly rising potential between a heavy quark and antiquark, with a "string" of colour field between them. It has not been derived analytically from the QCD equations; proving the associated mass gap is a Clay Millennium Prize problem.

facts: colourless: three quarks, three antiquarks, or a quark and an antiquark
yes: no isolated quark or gluon has ever been observed
open_questions: Confinement is seen in computer calculations of QCD but not proved from the equations (C2).

title: Asymptotic freedom
summary: The strong force gets weaker when quarks are very close or collide at high energy, which is why high-energy experiments can see quarks almost free.

layers.basics: Unlike electric forces, the strong force grows stronger as particles move apart and weaker as they get very close. At very high collision energies quarks inside a proton hardly feel each other and behave almost as free particles; this property is called asymptotic freedom. It is why scattering experiments at high energy can treat quarks as nearly independent points, and why calculations are possible there.
layers.deeper: The strength of the strong force is measured by a number αs that changes with the energy of the process: about 0.118 at the mass of the Z boson, smaller at higher energy, and large (around and above 1) near 1 GeV (PDG QCD review 2026: "αs ∼ 0.1 in the 0.1–1 TeV range, strongly interacting at and below 1 GeV"). The PDG notes that measurements of αs at many energies show this running exactly as QCD predicts.
layers.expert: At one loop the running is αs(Q) = αs(M_Z) / [1 + (b₀ αs(M_Z) / 2π) ln(Q/M_Z)], with b₀ = 11 − 2n_f/3. With n_f = 5 flavours b₀ = 23/3. The figure uses this one-loop form, which captures the trend but is not precise (PDG results use higher-order calculations). The 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Gross, Politzer and Wilczek for discovering asymptotic freedom.
