title: Where the proton's mass comes from
summary: Only about 1% of a proton's mass is the rest mass of its three quarks: most is the energy of the strong field and of the quarks' motion.

layers.basics:
A proton weighs 938 MeV/c². Its three valence quarks (two up, one down) have rest masses of only about 2, 2 and 5 MeV/c² (MS-bar values at 2 GeV, PDG): together about 9 MeV, roughly 1% of the proton. The rest comes from the energy of the quarks moving at high speed in a tiny space and from the energy of the gluon field that binds them: by E = mc², energy has mass.

So the Higgs boson does not supply most of your mass. It gives the quarks and electrons their small rest masses; the rest of the mass of ordinary matter comes from the strong force.
layers.deeper: Lattice QCD calculations decompose the proton mass into parts (a 2018 calculation by the χQCD collaboration, MS-bar scheme at 2 GeV): quark energy 33(4)(4)%, glue field energy 37(5)(4)%, a trace-anomaly part 23(1)(1)% and quark scalar-condensate (sigma) terms 9(2)(1)%. The pieces depend on how the mass is divided, so the exact split is a convention; what is robust is that the quark rest masses contribute only a few percent at most.
layers.expert: The decomposition uses the energy–momentum tensor: M = ⟨P|T⁰⁰|P⟩ separated into quark kinetic, gluon, quark mass and anomaly contributions. The sigma terms are the part that responds to changing the quark masses. Alternative decompositions (Ji; Jaffe–Manohar) assign the pieces differently; they are different bookkeeping of the same total.

facts: Rest masses of u, u, d
≈ 9 MeV, about 1% of the proton (sum of PDG MS-bar masses)
quark energy 33%, glue 37%, anomaly 23%, sigma terms 9%
open_questions: The split of the proton mass into parts depends on convention; the total is exact, the parts are not unique (C2).

title: Antimatter
summary: Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and opposite charges; when they meet they can annihilate into energy.

layers.basics:
For every particle there is an antiparticle: same mass and spin, opposite electric charge (and opposite colour, and so on). The antiparticle of the electron is the positron, found in cosmic rays by Carl Anderson in 1932. When a particle meets its antiparticle they can annihilate, turning into other particles such as photons: an electron and positron at rest make two photons of 511 keV each.

Some particles, like the photon, are their own antiparticles. For the neutrino, nobody knows yet.
layers.deeper: Antimatter is not exotic fuel in the world around you: positrons come from some radioactive decays, and PET scanners in hospitals use them. The universe, however, is made almost entirely of matter, not an even mix. The Standard Model has a small difference between matter and antimatter (CP violation) but far too little to explain this imbalance, an open question.
layers.expert: In quantum field theory antiparticles follow from combining quantum mechanics with special relativity (CPT symmetry: a particle and its antiparticle have exactly equal masses and lifetimes, and opposite charges). The PDG tests this: for example the proton and antiproton masses agree, and the charge-to-mass ratios agree, to high precision (see its listings).

facts: two photons of 0.511 MeV each when at rest (calculation from the electron mass)
why the universe is matter, not antimatter
open_questions: Why is there more matter than antimatter in the universe? (C3)

title: Spin, fermions and bosons
summary: Every particle has a built-in angular momentum called spin; whole-number spin particles carry forces and half-number ones make matter.

layers.basics:
Every particle has spin, an inherent amount of angular momentum. It is not a literal spinning ball: nothing is turning. Spin comes in fixed sizes. Quarks and leptons have spin ½ (fermions); the gluon, photon, W and Z have spin 1; the Higgs has spin 0 (bosons).

The split matters. Two identical fermions cannot occupy the same state (the Pauli exclusion principle), which is why electrons stack in shells in atoms and gives the periodic table its shape. Bosons can crowd into the same state, which is why many photons can make a laser beam.
layers.deeper: Spin is measured in units of ħ: ½ means the particle's spin along any chosen axis can only be +½ or −½. The photon, being massless, has two possible polarisations although it has spin 1.
layers.expert: The spin–statistics theorem links the two classes: spin-½ fields obey Fermi–Dirac statistics, integer spin fields Bose–Einstein. It follows from relativistic quantum field theory. The proton and neutron, made of three spin-½ quarks, are also fermions with spin ½; a pion, made of a quark and an antiquark, is a boson of spin 0.

title: Three generations
summary: Quarks and leptons come in three copies that differ only in mass: why three is not known.

layers.basics:
The quarks and leptons come in three generations, each a heavier copy of the one before. The first (up, down, electron, electron neutrino) makes everyday matter. The second (charm, strange, muon, muon neutrino) and the third (top, bottom, tau, tau neutrino) have the same charges and spins but larger masses, and their particles decay quickly into first-generation ones.

Nobody knows why there are three. Experiments on the Z boson show three light neutrinos, but cannot rule out heavier extra ones.
layers.deeper: The generations mix: weak decays can change a quark from one generation to another (described by the CKM matrix for quarks and the PMNS matrix for neutrinos). That mixing allows a difference between matter and antimatter in the Standard Model, which needs at least three generations.
layers.expert: The charges in each generation sum to zero when quark colours are counted: 3 × (+2/3) + 3 × (−1/3) + (−1) + 0 = 0. This cancellation (anomaly cancellation) is required for the theory to be consistent, and it is the reason leptons and quarks come together in complete generations.

open_questions: Why three generations, and why these masses? (C3, unexplained)

title: Neutrino oscillation
summary: A neutrino made as one kind can be detected later as another: proof that neutrinos have mass.

layers.basics:
A neutrino is created as one of three flavours (electron, muon or tau), but as it travels it can be detected as a different flavour. This oscillation happens because the flavours are mixtures of three states with slightly different masses; as the states travel they fall out of step. It means neutrinos have mass, which the original Standard Model did not allow.

The effect was shown by the Super-Kamiokande detector in 1998 (atmospheric neutrinos) and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory in 2001–2002 (solar neutrinos).
layers.deeper: Oscillation depends on the ratio of the distance travelled L to the neutrino energy E, and on the difference of the squared masses. The PDG 2026 values: Δm²₂₁ = (7.60 ± 0.17)×10⁻⁵ eV², |Δm²₃₂| ≈ 2.4–2.5×10⁻³ eV², and mixing angles sin²θ₁₂ = 0.307, sin²θ₁₃ = 0.0217, sin²θ₂₃ ≈ 0.53. JUNO, a reactor-neutrino experiment, has begun giving more precise results (see frontier file juno_oscillation).
layers.expert: In the two-flavour approximation the probability that a neutrino keeps its flavour after distance L (km) and energy E (GeV) is P = 1 − sin²2θ · sin²(1.267 Δm² L / E), with Δm² in eV². The figure uses this with the PDG atmospheric values as defaults. The full three-flavour formula involves a unitary PMNS matrix with a possible CP-violating phase δ = 1.21 (+0.19, −0.17) π rad (PDG 2026).

open_questions: Normal or inverted mass ordering? Absolute masses? Dirac or Majorana? (C3)
formula: P(ν → same flavour) = 1 − sin²2θ · sin²(1.267 Δm² [eV²] L [km] / E [GeV])

title: Beta decay
summary: A neutron turns into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino: the weak force changing a down quark into an up quark.

layers.basics:
In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. The electron's charge −1 balances the proton's +1, so total charge stays zero. A free neutron lasts about 878 seconds on average (about 14.6 minutes; PDG 2026: 878.3 ± 0.4 s); inside most stable nuclei neutrons are stable.

At the level of quarks, one of the neutron's two down quarks turns into an up quark by emitting a W⁻ boson, which immediately becomes an electron and an antineutrino. This is the weak force at work.
layers.deeper: The PDG average neutron lifetime has a scale factor of 1.8, which flags that the two measurement methods (counting neutrons in a bottle and counting decay protons in a beam) do not agree well: the so-called neutron lifetime puzzle. The neutron is heavier than the proton by 1.2933325 ± 0.0000004 MeV/c² (PDG), more than the electron's rest mass, so the decay is allowed.
layers.expert: Neutron decay is a mixed vector and axial-vector weak transition whose rates depend on the ratio of the axial to vector couplings, g_A/g_V, about 1.27. In the Sun's core a proton turns into a neutron in the step p + p → deuteron + e⁺ + νₑ; because it needs the weak force it is extremely slow, which is why the Sun burns for billions of years rather than all at once.

open_questions: Why do bottle and beam measurements of the neutron lifetime differ? (C3)

title: Conservation laws
summary: Some quantities (energy, momentum, electric charge, baryon number and lepton number) are the same before and after any reaction we have seen.

layers.basics:
In every decay and collision ever observed, certain totals are unchanged. Energy and momentum are conserved. So is electric charge: a neutron (0) becomes a proton (+1) plus an electron (−1). So is baryon number (quarks count +⅓, antiquarks −⅓), which is why a proton cannot simply vanish, and lepton number (leptons count +1, antileptons −1), which is why the neutron's decay comes with an antineutrino.

These rules decide which reactions can happen. They are bookkeeping that nature always balances.
layers.deeper: The table checks some real decays. Some conservation laws are exact as far as we know (charge, energy, momentum); others, like baryon and lepton number, have never been seen to fail but are not protected by a known deep reason, and proposed extensions of the Standard Model predict that proton decay should eventually be seen. The PDG limit on the proton lifetime is above 9×10²⁹ years.
layers.expert: Noether's theorem links each exact conservation law to a symmetry: energy to time translation, momentum to space translation, electric charge to a U(1) phase symmetry. Baryon and lepton number are "accidental" symmetries of the Standard Model Lagrangian (not imposed), broken by quantum effects in a way too small to see; B − L is exactly preserved in the model.

facts: Never seen to fail, no deep reason known

title: Feynman diagrams
summary: Feynman diagrams are bookkeeping for calculating how likely a reaction is: the lines are not paths that particles follow.

layers.basics:
A Feynman diagram is a picture used to organise a calculation. Lines for particles come in, meet at "vertices" where they interact, and lines go out. Each diagram stands for one term in a sum, and the more diagrams you add, the more precise the answer.

The lines are not literal paths. A quantum particle has no single path between start and end. And the particles on the inside of a diagram, called virtual, are not little balls: they are shorthand for terms in the maths.
layers.deeper: Time usually runs left to right. A line going backwards in time is the same as an antiparticle going forwards. At each vertex the conservation laws must hold: charge in equals charge out. The picture on this card is the simplest one: two electrons repel by exchanging one photon.
layers.expert: Each diagram is a recipe, via the Feynman rules, for a product of propagators and vertex factors. The sum of the diagrams for a process, to a given order in the coupling constant, gives the amplitude; squaring it gives the probability. "Virtual" particles are internal lines; they need not satisfy E² = p² + m² and are not directly observable.

facts: one term in a perturbation series
virtual particles: terms in a calculation, not observable balls

title: Virtual particles and the quark sea
summary: Virtual particles are terms in a calculation, not tiny balls popping in and out of existence; the proton's "sea" of quark–antiquark pairs is measured, but the flickering is a metaphor.

layers.basics:
You will see "virtual particles" described as little balls that pop into existence and vanish. That is a metaphor for something in the mathematics: the internal lines in a Feynman diagram, which are terms in a calculation that gives the chance of a reaction. You cannot detect one on its own.

Inside a proton the strong force and the energy of the field make a lively state. Scattering experiments show the proton holds more than its three valence quarks: it also contains extra quarks and antiquarks (the sea) and a great many gluons. The flickering pairs in this explorer's proton scene are a visual metaphor for that measured content: the true proton is one quantum state, not a collection of sparks.
layers.deeper: What is measured: in high-energy scattering, the proton shows quarks and antiquarks of several flavours and gluons carrying a large share of its momentum. At what scale and how you divide it matters; lattice QCD gives about half of the proton's momentum to gluons (51% at 2 GeV in a 2022 calculation).
layers.expert: The sea is described by parton distribution functions, extracted from fits to data from many experiments (PDG 2026 Structure Functions review). As the energy of the probe rises, more of the proton's momentum is found in gluons and sea quarks. A parton is a way of describing the state at one scale, not a particle with a definite path.

facts: u u d in the proton (net quantum numbers)
quark–antiquark pairs, with all flavours, in a proton (measured in scattering)
about 49% quarks and antiquarks, 51% gluons (lattice QCD, 2 GeV; scale dependent)

title: The proton
summary: A positively charged particle of two up quarks and one down quark; the nucleus of hydrogen and a building block of every nucleus.

layers.basics:
The proton is a particle of two up quarks and one down quark held by gluons. Its charge is +1 and its mass is 938.27 MeV/c², about 1,836 times the electron. It is about 0.84 femtometres (0.84×10⁻¹⁵ m) in radius: a hundred thousand times smaller than an atom. The nucleus of hydrogen is one proton; the number of protons decides what element an atom is.

Nobody has seen a proton decay: the PDG bound on its lifetime is more than 9×10²⁹ years.
layers.deeper: Only about 1% of its mass is the rest mass of its quarks; the rest is the energy of the strong field and of quark motion (see "Where the proton's mass comes from"). Besides the three valence quarks it holds a sea of quark–antiquark pairs and many gluons. The pictures of the proton in this explorer are cartoons: quarks have no measured size, nothing has a definite position and the picture is not to scale.
layers.expert: The PDG proton charge radius, 0.8407 ± 0.0006 fm, is a PDG average of measurements. Magnetic moment 2.7928473446(8) nuclear magnetons. In QCD the proton is the lowest-energy state with baryon number 1.

facts: no decay ever seen; mean life > 9×10²⁹ years (PDG, 90% CL)
open_questions: Does the proton ever decay? No decay seen; some extensions of the Standard Model say yes (C3).

title: The neutron
summary: An electrically neutral particle of one up quark and two down quarks; it lasts about 15 minutes when free.

layers.basics: The neutron is a particle of one up quark and two down quarks. Its charge is zero (⅔ − ⅓ − ⅓). It is a little heavier than the proton (939.565 against 938.272 MeV/c²), which lets a free neutron decay: in about 878 seconds on average it becomes a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. Inside most nuclei it is stable, and neutrons are what hold nuclei together without adding electric repulsion.
layers.deeper: Although neutral, the neutron has a magnetic moment (−1.913 nuclear magnetons), a sign that it holds moving charges: its quarks. The PDG gives a mean square charge radius of −0.1155 ± 0.0017 fm², negative, which is commonly read as the negative charge sitting further out than the positive. The neutron's extra mass comes mainly from the down quark being heavier than the up quark, partly offset by electromagnetic energy.
layers.expert: PDG 2026 neutron lifetime: 878.3 ± 0.4 s with a scale factor of 1.8 (the bottle and beam methods differ). The neutron electric dipole moment has not been seen; its tiny upper limit is part of the strong-CP problem.

facts: 0 (total: 2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3); PDG limit |q| consistent with zero, (−2 ± 8)×10⁻²² e

title: Hadrons: what else quarks can make
summary: Particles built from quarks come in two main kinds: baryons (three quarks, like the proton) and mesons (a quark and an antiquark).

layers.basics:
A hadron is any particle made of quarks held by the strong force. Baryons are three quarks, like the proton (uud) and the neutron (udd). Mesons are a quark with an antiquark, like the pion (up and anti-down) and the J/ψ (charm and anti-charm). The allowed combinations are the colourless ones (see "Colour charge and confinement"); more exotic hadrons with four or five quarks have been seen in recent years and are reviewed by the Particle Data Group.

Hundreds of hadrons are known; almost all decay quickly.
layers.deeper: The table lists a selection from the PDG 2026. Heavier hadrons (those with strange, charm or bottom quarks) decay by the weak force, living between about 10⁻¹³ and 10⁻⁸ seconds (for those in the table); some (like the Δ⁺⁺, which decays by the strong force) are "resonances" that last only about 6×10⁻²⁴ seconds (from its width of about 117 MeV; my calculation) and show up as bumps in collision data.
layers.expert: Hadron masses are mostly strong-field energy, not the sum of the quark masses: the pion (139.57 MeV/c²) is far lighter than a proton, because the pion is a near-massless Goldstone-like boson of chiral symmetry breaking. The charged pion mass is known to ±0.00018 MeV (PDG 2026).

facts: three quarks (e.g. uud, udd, uds, uuu, sss)
quark + antiquark (e.g. u d̄, c c̄)
four- and five-quark states have been reported (PDG pentaquark review)

title: The nuclear force and binding energy
summary: The force that holds protons and neutrons together in a nucleus is a leftover of the strong force, often described as exchange of pions.

layers.basics:
Inside a nucleus the protons repel each other electrically, yet nuclei hold together. What holds them is the residual strong force: a leftover of the force between quarks, like the weak attraction between neutral molecules left over from electric forces. It is often described as protons and neutrons swapping pions, which sets its range to about 1.4 femtometres (ħ divided by the pion mass times c; my calculation from the pion mass in the PDG).

The energy that would be needed to take a nucleus apart is its binding energy. Per particle it is largest for nuclei near iron and nickel, which is why fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones both release energy.
layers.deeper: Binding energy per nucleon from the AME2020 atomic mass evaluation: helium-4 7.07 MeV, carbon-12 7.68, oxygen-16 7.98, iron-56 8.79, nickel-62 8.79, uranium-238 7.57. Nickel-62 has the highest binding energy per nucleon of any nuclide in the table.
layers.expert: The pion-exchange picture goes back to Yukawa (1935): a force mediated by a particle of mass m has range about ħ/(mc). It is an effective description; modern chiral effective field theory builds the nuclear force from pion exchange plus short-range terms, derived from QCD's symmetries. In the picture of this explorer, the pion is a quark–antiquark meson and the exchange is a bookkeeping device.

facts: AME2020 (Wang et al., Chinese Physics C 45, 030003)

title: How we know: colliders and detectors
summary: Particles are found by smashing beams together and recording what comes out; most of the Standard Model was found that way.

layers.basics:
Most of what we know about particles comes from collisions. A collider accelerates beams of particles (electrons, protons, positrons, antiprotons) to near the speed of light and makes them collide. The energy of the collision turns into new particles (E = mc²). A detector built around the collision point surrounds it in layers: tracking chambers follow charged particles, calorimeters stop them and measure their energy, and outer chambers pick out muons.

Heavy and short-lived particles like the top quark, W, Z and Higgs are never seen directly: they are reconstructed from the particles they decay into.
layers.deeper: Discoveries in this explorer's data came this way: the J/ψ at SLAC and Brookhaven (1974), the gluon at PETRA (1979), the W and Z at CERN's proton–antiproton collider (1983), the top quark at Fermilab (1995) and the Higgs at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (2012). Cosmic rays gave the positron, muon and kaon before accelerators existed.
layers.expert: A "discovery" in particle physics is a statistical statement: a signal beyond a chosen number of standard deviations over the background (conventionally five). The PDG compiles the combined results of thousands of measurements into the numbers used here.

facts: SLAC SPEAR, DESY PETRA, CERN SPS, Fermilab Tevatron, CERN LHC
Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2026

title: Deep inelastic scattering
summary: Firing electrons at protons at high energy showed in 1968–69 that protons have small, hard constituents inside them.

layers.basics: If you fire high-energy electrons at protons and look at how they bounce, you can tell what is inside. At SLAC in 1968–69, electrons scattered off protons much more often at large angles than a smooth blob would allow: the proton had small, hard things inside. These were later identified with quarks. The method is called deep inelastic scattering.
layers.deeper: The PDG describes the measurements by two variables: Q², how hard the electron strikes, and x, the fraction of the proton's momentum carried by the struck constituent in the simple "parton" picture. Later experiments (such as HERA in Hamburg) mapped the proton's content from large to tiny x, finding rising numbers of gluons and sea quarks.
layers.expert: Structure functions F₂(x, Q²) depend only weakly on Q² in a range, "Bjorken scaling", as expected for pointlike constituents; the slow violations of scaling are the effect of gluon radiation predicted by QCD (PDG 2026 Structure Functions review).

facts: pointlike constituents (partons), later identified with quarks

title: The Higgs mechanism
summary: A field that has a nonzero value everywhere gives the W, Z, quarks and charged leptons their masses.

layers.basics:
The simplest equations for the W and Z bosons and for quarks and electrons have all of them massless. The Higgs field fixes that. It is a field that is not zero even in empty space. The W and Z, and the quarks and charged leptons, interact with it, and the interaction acts like a mass. The stronger a particle's coupling to the Higgs field, the heavier it is.

Photons and gluons do not interact with it and stay massless. The Higgs boson is a ripple of this field, and it was found in 2012.

Popular analogies (a crowd, treacle) are misleading: the Higgs field does not slow particles by friction.
layers.deeper:
The Higgs field's energy is lowest not at zero but at a nonzero value, v ≈ 246 GeV (PDG), a ring of equally good minima (the "Mexican hat"). The universe sits in one point on that ring: "spontaneous symmetry breaking".

The Higgs mechanism does not explain neutrino masses in the original model (neutrinos have no coupling to it there), nor most of ordinary mass (that comes from the strong force).
layers.expert: The complex SU(2) doublet φ has potential V(φ) = μ²φ†φ + (λ²/2)(φ†φ)² with μ² < 0 (PDG Electroweak Model review, eq. 10.1). The vacuum value breaks SU(2)×U(1) to U(1)em, gives W and Z masses m_W = g v/2 and m_Z = m_W / cos θ_W, and fermion masses via Yukawa couplings m_f = y_f v / √2. The 125 GeV Higgs boson's mass fixes λ, but the shape of the potential away from the minimum has not been measured.

open_questions: Is the Higgs potential the simple shape drawn here? Its form away from the minimum has not been measured (C3).

title: Gravity: the missing force
summary: Gravity is the one known force that the Standard Model does not include.

layers.basics:
Gravity shapes planets, stars and galaxies, but it plays no part in the Standard Model. Between two particles it is extraordinarily weak: the electric repulsion between two protons is about 10³⁶ times stronger than their gravitational attraction (my calculation from the constants). Gravity matters for big things because there is only one sign of mass, so it always adds up.

Einstein's general relativity describes gravity very well, but nobody has a quantum theory of it that has been tested. That is why the Standard Model view in this explorer shows gravity as the one missing interaction.
layers.deeper: If gravity has a force-carrying particle (a graviton), it has not been seen, and at the energies of any experiment its effects on single particles are far too small to measure. Ideas for combining gravity with quantum theory (string theory, loop quantum gravity and others) are not confirmed by experiment.
layers.expert: General relativity treats gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Treated as a quantum field theory like the others it gives infinities that cannot be removed in the usual way, so it works only as an effective theory at low energies. The energy where quantum effects of gravity become strong is far above anything reachable in a laboratory.

facts: Electric repulsion ÷ gravitational attraction, two protons
open_questions: A tested quantum theory of gravity does not exist (C3).

title: What the Standard Model leaves out
summary: The Standard Model has known gaps: gravity, dark matter, dark energy, neutrino masses, the matter–antimatter imbalance, and numbers it cannot predict.

layers.basics:
The Standard Model is very successful, and it is incomplete. It leaves out: gravity; dark matter (the extra, invisible mass that holds galaxies together, which none of the 17 particles can be); dark energy (the cause of the universe's accelerating expansion); neutrino masses (zero in the original model, not zero in nature); and why the universe contains matter rather than equal parts matter and antimatter.

It also has about 19 numbers it cannot predict, and cannot say why there are three generations of particles.
layers.deeper:
The 19: six quark masses, three charged-lepton masses, three quark-mixing angles and one CP-violating phase, three force strengths, two Higgs parameters and one strong-CP angle. Neutrino masses and mixing add more. The count depends on convention.

The certainty tag of each item is shown with it on the figure. Most experts expect the model to be an effective description that fails at higher energies; where and how it fails is unknown.
layers.expert: The Higgs mass hierarchy problem and the strong CP problem are "naturalness" puzzles: parameters that are, in the model, oddly small. The PDG's review of compositeness finds no structure inside quarks or electrons down to roughly 10⁻¹⁹ to 10⁻²⁰ m (contact-interaction scale Λ above about 9–36 TeV; model dependent; length ħc/Λ is about 5×10⁻²¹ to 2×10⁻²⁰ m by my calculation).

open_questions: Gravity (C3): The Standard Model has no gravity. General relativity describes it very well, but nobody has a tested quantum theory of it; the two descriptions have not been joined.

Dark matter (C2): Motions of stars, galaxies and clusters, and the pattern of the early universe, indicate matter that does not shine; none of the 17 particles fits (neutrinos are too light). What it is remains unknown.
Dark energy (C3): The expansion of the universe is accelerating. The Standard Model has no explanation, and the vacuum energy it would naturally predict is far larger than what is observed.

Neutrino masses (C1): The original Standard Model had massless neutrinos. Oscillation proves they have mass, so the model had to be extended; how neutrinos get their mass, and whether they are Majorana particles, is not known.

Matter–antimatter imbalance (C2): Matter and antimatter should have been made equally in the Big Bang, yet the universe is made of matter. The known sources of CP violation in the Standard Model are far too small to explain the amount.

Why three generations (C3): Why there are three copies of the quark and lepton pattern, and not two or four, is not known. Experiments on Z decay show three light neutrino kinds, but say nothing about heavier ones.

Free parameters (C3): The model contains about 19 numbers that are not predicted but must be measured (the masses, the mixing angles, the force strengths and so on; see the count below). Why they have the values they have is unexplained.

Why the Higgs is so light (C3): Quantum corrections would naturally push the Higgs mass towards the highest energy scale in the theory. That it stays at 125 GeV is called the hierarchy problem; no accepted solution has been confirmed.

The strong CP problem (C3): The strong force could violate the matter–antimatter mirror symmetry (the parameter θ), but measurements of the neutron's electric dipole moment find it indistinguishable from zero. Why it is so small is unexplained.

Are quarks and electrons really pointlike? (C2): No internal structure has been found. PDG 2026 reports limits on a compositeness scale of roughly 10 to 35 TeV, which corresponds to sizes below about 10⁻²⁰ m. That is a limit of measurement, not a proof that there is nothing inside.
